e-485.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Linear Polynomials
e-485.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

|  | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}-1$ | $4$ | $-1$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $-4$ |
|  | $4$ | $-5$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\dfrac{4x-1}{x+1} = 4 -\dfrac{5}{x+1}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{4x-1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(4-\frac{5}{x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}4\,\text{d}x-5{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4x{|}_{0}^{1}-5\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[4-0]-5[\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\operatorname{ln}⁡1] \\  & =4-5\operatorname{ln}⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

e-486.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator is Linear
e-486.worked_solution:
We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division. 

We draw up a synthetic division table:

|  | $x^2$ | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}3$ | $2$ | $-3$ | $-4$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $6$ | $9$ |
|  | $2$ | $3$ | $5$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\eqalign{
		\dfrac{ 2x^2-3x-4}{x-3} = 2x + 3 + \dfrac {5}{x-3} .
	}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2{x}^{2}-3x-4}{x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+3+\frac{5}{x-3})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}+3x+5\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

e-487.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator Contains a Leading Coefficient
e-487.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{2(x-\frac{1}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{1}{2})}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

|  | $x^1$ | $x^0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $\color{red}\dfrac12$ | $1$ | $-1$ |
|  | $\color{gray}\downarrow$ | $\dfrac12$ |
|  | $1$ | $-\dfrac12$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{1}{2})} & =1-\frac{(\frac{1}{2})}{(x-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2(x-\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{2x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{1}{2x-1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|]+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x-1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since x+3=(x-4)+7, the integrand is 1+7/(x-4). Integrating gives x+7 ln|x-4|+C.

after.name: Question 1
after.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ 4 & 1 & 3 \\  & ↓ & 4 \\  & 1 & 7\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{x+3}{x-4}=1+\frac{7}{x-4}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+3}{x-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{7}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+7\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+7\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Linear Polynomials
content.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ 4 & 1 & 3 \\  & ↓ & 4 \\  & 1 & 7\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{x+3}{x-4}=1+\frac{7}{x-4}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x+3}{x-4}\,\text{d}x & =\int (1+\frac{7}{x-4})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \text{d}x+7\int \frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x+7\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 2
after.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

|  | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-1$ | $7$ | $4$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-7$ |
|  | $7$ | $-3$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{7x+4}{x+1}=7-\frac{3}{x+1}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{7x+4}{x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(7-\frac{3}{x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =7{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x-3{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{x+1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =7x\,{|}_{0}^{2}-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+1|\,{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =7(2-0)-3(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+1|) \\  & =14-3(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡1) \\  & =14-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(\,3\,).\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since 2x-3=2(x-1)-1, the integrand is 2-1/(x-1). Thus the integral is [2x-ln|x-1|] from 2 to 3, which equals 2-ln(2).

after.name: Question 3
after.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ 1 & 2 & -3 \\  & ↓ & 2 \\  & 2 & -1\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{2x-3}{x-1}=2-\frac{1}{x-1}.
$$

Therefore,

$$

after.name: Question 4
after.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & 5 & 7 \\  & ↓ & -10 \\  & 5 & -3\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{5x+7}{x+2}=5-\frac{3}{x+2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$

xx0−257↓−105−3

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Linear Polynomials
content.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & 5 & 7 \\  & ↓ & -10 \\  & 5 & -3\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{5x+7}{x+2}=5-\frac{3}{x+2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5x+7}{x+5}\,\text{d}x & =\int (5-\frac{3}{x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =5\int \text{d}x-3\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =5x-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since (x+4)/(x+3)=1+1/(x+3), the integral is [x+ln|x+3|] from -2 to 0. This equals ln(3)-(-2+ln(1))=2+ln(3).

after.name: Question 5
after.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & 1 & 4 \\  & ↓ & -3 \\  & 1 & 1\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{x+4}{x+3}=1+\frac{1}{x+3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{0}\frac{x+4}{x+3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}(1+\frac{1}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\text{d}x+{\int }_{-2}^{0}\frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{|}_{-2}^{0}+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =(0-(-2))+(\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|-2+3|) \\  & =2+\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Quotient of Linear Polynomials
content.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder. For this, we can use synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & 1 & 4 \\  & ↓ & -3 \\  & 1 & 1\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{x+4}{x+3}=1+\frac{1}{x+3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-2}^{0}\frac{x+4}{x+3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}(1+\frac{1}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}\text{d}x+{\int }_{-2}^{0}\frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{|}_{-2}^{0}+\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|{|}_{-2}^{0} \\  & =(0-(-2))+(\operatorname{ln}⁡|0+3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|-2+3|) \\  & =2+\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 6
?

Calculate ∫3x3−9x2+x−1x−3dx.

a
13x3−3x2+2x−ln⁡|x−3|+C
b
13x3−3x−2ln⁡|x−3|+C
c
x3−9x2+x+ln⁡|x−3|+C
d
13x3−92x2+12x−3ln⁡|x−3|+C
e
x3+x+2ln⁡|x−3|+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Polynomial division gives (3x^3-9x^2+x-1)/(x-3)=3x^2+1+2/(x-3). Integrating term by term yields x^3+x+2 ln|x-3|+C.

after.name: Question 6
after.worked_solution:
We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 3 & 3 & -9 & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & 9 & 0 & 3 \\  & 3 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{3{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+x-1}{x-3}=3{x}^{2}+1+\frac{2}{x-3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+x-1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}+1+\frac{2}{x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =3\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+\int \text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}+x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

a

b

EXPLANATION

We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

x3x2x1x033−91−1↓9033012

So from the synthetic division, we get that

3x3−9x2+x−1x−3=3x2+1+2x−3.

Therefore,

∫3x3−9x2+x−1x−3dx=∫(3x2+1+2x−3)dx=3∫x2dx+∫dx+2∫1x−3dx=x3+x+2ln⁡|x−3|+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator is Linear
content.worked_solution:
We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 3 & 3 & -9 & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & 9 & 0 & 3 \\  & 3 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{3{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+x-1}{x-3}=3{x}^{2}+1+\frac{2}{x-3}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{3}-9{x}^{2}+x-1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}+1+\frac{2}{x-3})\text{d}x \\  & =3\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+\int \text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{3}+x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
The denominator of the integrand doesn't divide the numerator exactly, so we need to decompose it into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We start by drawing up our synthetic division table:

|  | ${x}^{3}$ | ${x}^{2}$ | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $-2$ | $1$ | $3$ | $2$ | $5$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-2$ | $-2$ | $0$ |
|  | $1$ | $1$ | $0$ | $5$ |

So, from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}+2x+5}{x+2}={x}^{2}+x+\frac{5}{x+2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{x}^{3}+3{x}^{2}+2x+5}{x+2}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}+x+\frac{5}{x+2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x+5{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}{|}_{0}^{1}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}{|}_{0}^{1}+5\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2}+5(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡2) \\  & =\frac{5}{6}+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2}) \\  & =\frac{5}{6}+5\operatorname{ln}⁡(\,\frac{3}{2}\,).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

∫3x2−2x+1x−1dx=

a
3x2−x+2ln⁡|x−1|+C
b
3x2+x−ln⁡|x−1|+C
c
x2−2x−4ln⁡|x−1|+C
d
32x2+x+4ln⁡|x−1|+C
e
32x2+x+2ln⁡|x−1|+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Polynomial division gives (3x^2-2x+1)/(x-1)=3x+1+2/(x-1). Integrating yields (3/2)x^2+x+2 ln|x-1|+C.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\  & ↓ & 3 & 1 \\  & 3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{3{x}^{2}-2x+1}{x-1}=3x+1+\frac{2}{x-1}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}-2x+1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3x+1+\frac{2}{x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =3\int x\,\text{d}x+\int \text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

∫3x2−2x+1x−1dx=

a
3x2−x+2ln⁡|x−1|+C
b
3x2+x−ln⁡|x−1|+C
c
x2−2x−4ln⁡|x−1|+C

32x2+x+4ln⁡|x−1|+C
e
32x2+x+2ln⁡|x−1|+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table: x2x1x013−21↓31312

So from the synthetic division, we get that 3x2−2x+1x−1=3x+1+2x−1.

Therefore,

∫3x2−2x+1x−1dx=∫(3x+1+2x−1)dx=3∫xdx+∫dx+2∫1x−1dx=32x2+x+2ln⁡|x−1|+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator is Linear
content.worked_solution:
We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ 1 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\  & ↓ & 3 & 1 \\  & 3 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{3{x}^{2}-2x+1}{x-1}=3x+1+\frac{2}{x-1}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3{x}^{2}-2x+1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\int (3x+1+\frac{2}{x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =3\int x\,\text{d}x+\int \text{d}x+2\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+x+2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

∫x3−3x2−x+2x+2dx=

a
13x3−52x2+9x−16ln⁡|x+2|+C
b
13x3−52x2+3x−4ln⁡|x+2|+C
c
13x3+3x2+x−2ln⁡|x+2|+C
d
x3−x2−12x−3ln⁡|x+2|+C
e
x3−3x2−x+2ln⁡|x+2|+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Polynomial division gives x^2-5x+9-16/(x+2). Integrating term by term gives x^3/3-(5/2)x^2+9x-16 ln|x+2|+C.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & 1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\  & ↓ & -2 & 10 & -18 \\  & 1 & -5 & 9 & -16\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-x+2}{x+2}={x}^{2}-5x+9-\frac{16}{x+2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-x+2}{x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-5x+9-\frac{16}{x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-5\int x\,\text{d}x+9\int \text{d}x-16\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}+9x-16\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

x3x2x1x0−21−3−12↓−210−181−59−16

x3−3x2−x+2x+2=x2−5x+9−16x+2.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator is Linear
content.worked_solution:
We first need to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder parts, which we can do using synthetic division.

We draw up a synthetic division table:

$$
\begin{aligned} & {x}^{3} & {x}^{2} & {x}^{1} & {x}^{0} \\ -2 & 1 & -3 & -1 & 2 \\  & ↓ & -2 & 10 & -18 \\  & 1 & -5 & 9 & -16\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-x+2}{x+2}={x}^{2}-5x+9-\frac{16}{x+2}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{3}-3{x}^{2}-x+2}{x+2}\,\text{d}x & =\int ({x}^{2}-5x+9-\frac{16}{x+2})\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x-5\int x\,\text{d}x+9\int \text{d}x-16\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}-\frac{5}{2}{x}^{2}+9x-16\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The integrand equals 3/2-(17/2)/(2x+3). Its antiderivative is 3x/2-(17/4)ln|2x+3|. Evaluating from 0 to 2 gives 3-(17/4)ln(7/3).

after.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2(x+\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{(x+\frac{3}{2})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -\frac{3}{2} & 3 & -4 \\  & ↓ & -\frac{9}{2} \\  & 3 & -\frac{17}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3x-4}{(x+\frac{3}{2})} & =3-\frac{(\frac{17}{2})}{(x+\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =3-\frac{17}{2(x+\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =3-\frac{17}{2x+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{3x-4}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(3-\frac{17}{2x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[3{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x-17{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2x+3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[3x-\frac{17}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+3|]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[3(2-0)-\frac{17}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2(2)+3|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2(0)+3|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[6-\frac{17}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡7-\operatorname{ln}⁡3)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[6-\frac{17}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{3})] \\  & =3-\frac{17}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{7}{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12

Calculate ∫x−12x+6dx.

a
x+2ln⁡|x+3|+C
b
x4+ln⁡|x+3|+C
c
x2−2ln⁡|x+3|+C

x−2ln⁡|x+3|+C

 x2−4ln⁡|x+3|+C

decision.explanation: Since x-1=(x+3)-4, the integrand equals 1/2-2/(x+3). Integrating gives x/2-2 ln|x+3|+C.

after.name: Question 12
after.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x+6}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{2(x+3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x-1}{(x+3)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & -3 \\  & 1 & -4\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x+3)} & =1+\frac{(-4)}{(x+3)} \\  & =1-\frac{4}{(x+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x+6}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{4}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

Calculate ∫x−12x+6dx.

a
x+2ln⁡|x+3|+C
b
x4+ln⁡|x+3|+C
c
x2−2ln⁡|x+3|+C
d
x−2ln⁡|x+3|+C
e
 x2−4ln⁡|x+3|+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we pull out the factor of 2 from the denominator:

∫x−12x+6dx=∫x−12(x+3)dx=12∫x−1(x+3)dx

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

xx0−31−1↓−31−4

So from the synthetic division, we get that

x−1(x+3)=1+(−4)(x+3)=1−4(x+3)

Therefore,

∫x−12x+6dx=12∫(1−4x+3)dx=12[∫dx−4∫1x+3dx]=12[x−4ln⁡|x+3|]+C=x2−2ln⁡|x+3|+C.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms the integrand equals 1/2-2/(x+3), giving x/2-2 ln|x+3|+C. Its derivative is (x-1)/(2x+6), so option c is correct.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator Contains a Leading Coefficient
content.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x+6}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{2(x+3)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{x-1}{(x+3)}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ -3 & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & -3 \\  & 1 & -4\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x+3)} & =1+\frac{(-4)}{(x+3)} \\  & =1-\frac{4}{(x+3)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{2x+6}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\frac{4}{x+3})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\int \text{d}x-4\int \frac{1}{x+3}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[x-4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+3|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Calculate ∫x−13x−2dx.

a
 x3+13ln⁡|3x−2|+C
b
 x−19ln⁡|3x−2|+C
c
 x−9ln⁡|3x−2|+C
d
x3−19ln⁡|3x−2|+C
e
 3x+9ln⁡|3x−2|+C
Submit

decision.explanation: Since x-1=(3x-2)/3-1/3, the integrand is 1/3-1/[3(3x-2)]. Integrating gives x/3-(1/9)ln|3x-2|+C.

after.name: Question 13
after.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $3$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{3(x-\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & \frac{2}{3} \\  & 1 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})} & =1+\frac{(-\frac{1}{3})}{(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3x-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int (1-\frac{1}{3x-2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\int \text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ∫x−13x−2dx.

a
 x3+13ln⁡|3x−2|+C
b
 x−19ln⁡|3x−2|+C
c
 x−9ln⁡|3x−2|+C
d
x3−19ln⁡|3x−2|+C
e
 3x+9ln⁡|3x−2|+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we pull out the factor of 3 from the denominator:

∫x−13x−2dx=∫x−13(x−23)dx=13∫x−1(x−23)dx

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

xx0231−1↓231−13

So from the synthetic division, we get that

x−1(x−23)=1+(−13)(x−23)=1−13(x−23)=1−13x−2.

Therefore,

∫x−13x−2dx=13∫(1−13x−2)dx=13[∫dx−∫13x−2dx]=13[x−13ln⁡|3x−2|]+C=x3−19ln⁡|3x−2|+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Function Whose Denominator Contains a Leading Coefficient
content.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $3$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{x-1}{3(x-\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})}\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{2}{3} & 1 & -1 \\  & ↓ & \frac{2}{3} \\  & 1 & -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})} & =1+\frac{(-\frac{1}{3})}{(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3(x-\frac{2}{3})} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3x-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{x-1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int (1-\frac{1}{3x-2})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\int \text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{3x-2}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[x-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|]+C \\  & =\frac{x}{3}-\frac{1}{9}\operatorname{ln}⁡|3x-2|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $4$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4(x-\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{(x-\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{1}{4} & 8 & 1 \\  & ↓ & 2 \\  & 8 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8x+1}{(x-\frac{1}{4})} & =8+\frac{3}{(x-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =8+\frac{12}{4x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}(8+\frac{12}{4x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\text{d}x+12{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8x+3\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x-1|]_{-1/8}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8(0-(-\frac{1}{8}))+3(\operatorname{ln}⁡|4(0)-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|4(-\frac{1}{8})-1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8(\frac{1}{8})+3(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2}))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[1-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})].\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $4$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4(x-\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{(x-\frac{1}{4})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

$$
\begin{aligned} & x & {x}^{0} \\ \frac{1}{4} & 8 & 1 \\  & ↓ & 2 \\  & 8 & 3\end{aligned}
$$

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8x+1}{(x-\frac{1}{4})} & =8+\frac{3}{(x-\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =8+\frac{12}{4x-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{8x+1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}(8+\frac{12}{4x-1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\text{d}x+12{\int }_{-1/8}^{0}\frac{1}{4x-1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8x+3\operatorname{ln}⁡|4x-1|]_{-1/8}^{0} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8(0-(-\frac{1}{8}))+3(\operatorname{ln}⁡|4(0)-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|4(-\frac{1}{8})-1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[8(\frac{1}{8})+3(\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2}))] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[1-3\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{2})].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 15
after.worked_solution:
First, we pull out the factor of $2$ from the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-1}{2(x+\frac{1}{2})}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we draw up our synthetic division table to decompose the integrand into its quotient and remainder.

|  | ${x}^{1}$ | ${x}^{0}$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $-\frac{1}{2}$ | $5$ | $-1$ |
|  | $↓$ | $-\frac{5}{2}$ |
|  | $5$ | $-\frac{7}{2}$ |

So from the synthetic division, we get that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5x-1}{(x+\frac{1}{2})} & =5-\frac{(\frac{7}{2})}{(x+\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =5-\frac{7}{2(x+\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =5-\frac{7}{2x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{5x-1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(5-\frac{7}{2x+1})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[5{\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}x-7{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2x+1}\,\text{d}x] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[5x{|}_{0}^{2}-\frac{7}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|2x+1|{|}_{0}^{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[5(2-0)-\frac{7}{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡|2\cdot 2+1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|2\cdot 0+1|)] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[10-\frac{7}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡5] \\  & =5-\frac{7}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡5.\end{aligned}
$$
